d.g: Any of various insects of the order Dermaptera that have elongated bodies, large membranous wings folded underneath short leathery forewings and a pair of large pincers protruding from the rear of the abdomen.
d.x: "That's a fine young fellow," said the historiographer of earwigs, to an American who stood next him in the crowd.

d.g: One who whispers insinuations; a secret counsellor.
d.x: That gawdy earwig, or my lord your patron, Whose pensioner you are.

d.g: A flatterer.
To fill the mind of with prejudice by insinuations.

earwig.e: From Middle English erwigge, from Old English ēarwicga, from ēare (“ear”) + wicga (“insect”), so named from the appearance of the hindwings, which are unique in their resemblance to human ears when unfolded.

d.g: plural of ea
Lack of difficulty; the ability to do something easily.
d.x: He played the ukelele with ease.

d.g: Freedom from pain, hardship, and annoyance, sometimes (derogatory, archaic) idleness, sloth.
d.x: She enjoyed the ease of living in a house where the servants did all the work.

d.g: Freedom from worry and concern; peace; sometimes (derogatory, archaic) indifference.
d.x: The pension set her mind at ease.

d.g: Freedom from effort; leisure, rest.
d.x: We took our ease on the patio.

ease.e: From Middle English ese, eise, aise, from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (“elbow room; opportunity”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais, Italian agio and asio, Sicilian aciu and Portuguese azo. …

d.g: An upright frame, typically on three legs, for displaying or supporting something, such as an artist's canvas.
d.x: Chevalet, (chaſſis de bois ſur lequel les Peintres poſent leurs Tableaux quand ils travaillent) a Painter's Eaſel.

easel.e: Borrowed from Dutch ezel (“donkey; easel”), from Middle Dutch esel (“donkey”), from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Latin asellus (“young ass or small donkey”), diminutive of asinus (“ass, donkey”), ultimately from an unknown source in Asia Minor. …

d.g: An interest in land which grants the legal right to use another person's real property (real estate), generally in order to cross a part of the property or to gain access to something on the property (right of way).
d.x: The power company has an easement to put their electricity poles along the edge of this land.

d.g: An element such as a baseboard, handrail, etc., that is curved instead of abruptly changing direction.
d.x: The curved part of the rail where it joins the newel is called an easement. Often, however, the rail joins the newel without an easement.

d.g: Transition spiral curve track between a straight or tangent track and a circular curved track of a certain radius or selected radius.
Gratification.

easement.e: From Anglo-Norman aisement, easement, eisement, esament, esement, and Middle French aisement (“comfort, convenience, ease, facility, opportunity; a benefit, relief; a right to use land, a thing, etc.; a privy”), from aisier (“to put at ease; to facilitate”) + -ment (“-ment, suffix forming nouns, usually the action or s …

d.g: Lack of difficulty; quality of not being frustrating, difficult, or dense (compact).
Looseness or pliancy, often derogatory
Freedom from discomfort and worry: comfort.
Freedom from inhibition and awkwardness: grace.

easiness.e: English easy Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English easiness From easy + -ness.

d.g: present participle and gerund of ease
The act by which something is eased.
d.x: Then everyone moved at the same time — slight shiftings of the hands and feet, furtive easings of position.

d.g: Eastern.
d.x: In the mean while, as our apartment was a corner one, and looked both east and north, I ran to the easter casement to look after Drummond.

d.g: comparative form of east: more east
An easterly wind (a wind blowing from the east); especially, a strong one; a storm of such winds.
d.x: A northeaster in one place may be an easter, a norther, or a souther in some other locality.

d.g: To move toward the east.
d.x: Off Tilbury the Alcyone's topsail-yard was carried away just forward of the slings; she set a jib-headed one; at Thames Haven the wind eastered ...

easter.e: From Old English eastera, eastra. Compare norther, souther, wester.

d.g: A native or inhabitant of the east of a region (or of the world as a whole), such as one of the eastern United States.

easterner.e: English eastern Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English easterner From eastern + -er.

d.g: the Easter season

United States inventor of a dry-plate process of developing photographic film and of flexible film (his firm introduced roll film) and of the box camera and of a process for color photography (1854-1932)
The quality of being easygoing.
d.x: Democratic or not, there is a certain easygoingness in Asmara, at least on the surface.

d.g: Edible growth of grass for horses and cattle, especially that of lattermath.
The right to let one's animals eat in a certain place; pasturage.
food

eatage.e: From a corruption (as if < eat + -age) of edige, eddish. More at eddish.

d.g: A person or animal who eats.
d.x: a very fussy eater

d.g: A fruit or other food that is suitable for eating, especially one that is intended to be eaten uncooked.
d.x: The bass is a fine eater.

d.g: A configuration of cells that appears to consume another configuration by gradually causing it to disappear.
d.x: The eater can also destroy a snail, but changes its phase while doing so.

eater.e: From Middle English eter, etere, etter, from Old English etere; equivalent to eat + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (patient suffix) (food suitable for eating).

d.g: A restaurant or café; a place to purchase and eat food.

eatery.e: English eat Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -ārius Old French -ier Proto-Indo-European *-yós Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Old French -ie Old French -eriebor. Middle English -erie English -ery English eatery From eat + -ery.

d.g: present participle and gerund of eat
Bred to be eaten.
d.x: eating chickens; eating quails

d.g: Suitable to be eaten without being cooked.
d.x: Wait! That's not an eating apple.

d.g: The act of ingesting food.
d.x: Arabs consider the eating of mushrooms as an aphrodisiac aid.

eating.e: From Middle English etynge, from Old English eting.

d.g: third-person singular simple present indicative of eat
Food.
d.x: When are we going to get some eats?

d.g: The underside of a roof that extends beyond the external walls of a building.
d.x: Him that you term'd Sir, the good old Lord Gonzallo, / His teares runs downe his beard like winters drops / From eaues of reeds: […]

d.g: Something that extends over or projects beyond.
d.x: But after many strains and heaves / He got up to the Saddle eaves.

d.g: plural of eave

eaves.e: PIE word *upér From Middle English eves (“projecting lower edge of a roof”) [and other forms], from Old English efes, yfes, *ofes (“edge of a roof”), from Proto-West Germanic *ubisu (“hall”), from Proto-Germanic *ubiswō (compare Gothic 𐌿𐌱𐌹𐌶𐍅𐌰 (ubizwa), Old High German obasa (“hall; porch; roof”)), perhaps ultimat …

d.g: One who eavesdrops.
A surveillance aircraft.

eavesdropper.e: English eavesdrop Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English eavesdropper From eavesdrop + -er (“person or thing which does”).

d.g: To gain (success, reward, recognition) through applied effort or work.
d.x: You can have the s'mores: you earned them, clearing the walkway of snow so well.

d.g: To receive payment for work or for a role or position held (regardless of whether effort was applied or whether the remuneration is deserved or commensurate).
d.x: He earns seven million dollars a year as CEO.  My bank account is only earning one percent interest.

d.g: To receive payment for work.
d.x: Now that you are earning, you can start paying me rent.

d.g: To cause (someone) to receive payment or reward.
d.x: My CD earns me six percent!

earn.e: From Middle English ernen, from Old English earnian, from Proto-West Germanic *aʀanōn, from Proto-Germanic *azanōną. This verb is denominal from the noun *azaniz (“harvest”).

d.g: To consume (something solid or semi-solid, usually food) by putting it into the mouth and swallowing it.
d.x: He's eating an apple. / Don't disturb me now; can't you see that I'm eating?

d.g: To consume a meal.
d.x: What time do we eat this evening?

d.g: To be eaten.
d.x: It's a soup that eats like a meal.

d.g: To have a particular quality of diet; to be well-fed or underfed (typically as "eat healthy" or "eat good").

eat.e: From Middle English eten, from Old English etan (“to eat”), from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną (“to eat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti, from *h₁ed- (“to eat”). …

d.g: To hear (intentionally) a conversation one is not intended to hear; to listen in.
d.x: I hope nobody was eavesdropping on our conversation last night, since it got so personal.

d.g: To listen for another organism's calls, so as to exploit them.
d.x: […] Eastern Red Bat will eavesdrop on the sonar calls of other red bats to locate potential insect prey.

d.g: The dripping of rain from the eaves of a house.
The space around a house on which such water drips.

eavesdrop.e: From eaves + drop; the "listening" sense derives from the notion of the listener standing in the area denoted by the physical sense.
